title: Low Dissolved Oxygen Favors Biological Phosphorus Removal, and Oxygen Inhibition of PAOs Is an Important Part of the Story
content:
Low dissolved oxygen (DO) operation improved biological phosphorus removal, whereas elevated DO concentrations inhibit polyphosphate-accumulating organism activity. Kinetic parameter estimation and functional gene prediction provided evidence that challenges conventional EBPR DO guidance and provides a new mechanistic framework linking oxygen inhibition to oxidative stress and polyphosphate formation.


ABSTRACT

Conventional enhanced biological phosphorus removal (EBPR) design assumes dissolved oxygen (DO) concentrations between 2 and 4 mg/L are required to support reliable phosphorus removal, despite limited mechanistic evidence establishing the DO requirements of polyphosphate-accumulating organisms (PAOs). This study evaluated long-term EBPR performance, PAO oxygen kinetics, and predicted functional genes under high and low DO conditions. EBPR performance remained stable and improved at low DO, with median effluent orthophosphate concentrations at 0.2 mg DO/L 40% lower and less variable than at 2.0 mg DO/L. Batch testing revealed extremely low PAO oxygen half-saturation coefficients (KDO < 0.1 mg/L) and maximum phosphorus uptake rates at low DO, whereas elevated DO hindered phosphorus uptake. This inhibitory behavior was described using the Andrews model, indicating that high concentrations of DO can suppress PAO activity. Exploratory functional prediction from 16S rRNA gene data indicated differences in predicted stress-response and polyphosphate-related gene content between DO conditions, which identify candidate genes for future gene expression studies. These findings challenge conventional design guidance and motivate direct investigation of PAO oxygen inhibition.
